awd_titl_txt: Travel: NSF Student Travel Grant for 2025 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV)
awd_abstract_narration:
This grant partially supports the participation of Ph.D. students from US institutions in the Doctoral Consortium at the 2025 IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV). WACV is the premier annual conference focused on the applications of computer vision. It is held in the United States and attended by members of the international research community. The goal of the PhD Forum is to highlight the work of PhD students working in computer vision and to give these students an opportunity to discuss their research and career options with senior researchers in the field. The broader impacts of this project include supporting the career development of some of the brightest junior researchers in computer vision, contributing to the research community in general by drawing attention to an important aspect of graduate student development, potentially increasing the number of active researchers and educators in STEM, and ensuring that the computer vision community, through its recent graduates, makes fast advances in solving problems that will benefit society as a whole. The Doctoral Consortium aims to have representation from a diverse group of participants in terms of gender, ethnic background, academic institution, and geographic location.

Support from the National Science Foundation covers some of the costs for 17 selected US-based graduate students to attend the conference. The selection of participants receiving travel support is conducted by the 2025 WACV Doctoral Consortium Chairs. For graduate students, this event offers a chance to receive guidance on their research and career plans from experts from various institutions, potentially offering diverse perspectives compared to their own research advisor. For senior researchers involved, the event serves as an opportunity to engage in meaningful discussions with promising young researchers and to contribute to the community through mentorship. This year's Doctoral Consortium features a poster session, one-on-one mentoring, and a panel discussion.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project supported student participation in the 2025 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV) through an NSF Student Travel Grant, with the goal of strengthening graduate education, mentorship, and community engagement in computer vision. The award enabled Ph.D. students—particularly those from institutions with limited travel resources—to attend a major international research conference and to participate in a dedicated Doctoral Consortium focused on professional development and scholarly exchange.

A central outcome of the project was the successful organization and execution of the WACV 2025 Doctoral Consortium, held on March 2, 2025. The consortium brought together 12 Ph.D. student mentees from 9 U.S. universities, and 16 senior mentors from academia and industry. During the two-hour event, participants engaged in structured roundtable discussions and poster-based mentoring sessions. Students presented their thesis research, received individualized feedback on research direction and methodology, and discussed career pathways spanning academia, industry, and applied research.

From an intellectual merit perspective, the project contributed to the development of the computer vision discipline by providing opportunities to present,discuss, and receive feedback on original research within the broader community. The WACV conference provides a venue to foster such meaningful interchanges between researchers and facilitate graduate student development. Direct feedback from experienced researchers helped students improve the clarity, rigor, and impact of their work at a formative stage, influencing future publications and dissertation outcomes. By integrating mentors from both academic and industrial backgrounds, the consortium also encouraged students to consider real-world relevance and translational impact alongside theoretical advances.

Broader Impacts. The project was designed to broaden participation and expand access to high-quality professional development opportunities in computer vision. As the applicant pool permitted, the Doctoral Consortium included participants from a diverse range of backgrounds in terms of gender, ethnic background, academic institution, and geographic location, with travel awards granted on the basis of students’ thesis research and demonstrated need. The most immediate beneficiaries were Ph.D. students for whom NSF support made conference attendance possible, enabling them to engage fully in mentoring, networking, and scholarly exchange.The consortium fostered cross-institutional mentorship and networking, helping students build lasting professional relationships beyond their home institutions. These connections are expected to support students’ long-term success and retention in the STEM workforce.

More broadly, the Doctoral Consortium benefited the WACV conference and the computer vision research community by highlighting the critical role of graduate student development and mentorship in sustaining a healthy research ecosystem. By strengthening early-career training and fostering inclusive participation, the project contributes to the continued growth and impact of WACV and, in turn, supports the broader scientific community and public interest as computer vision research plays an increasingly important role in applications involving digital images, video, and visual understanding across society. 

The project also supported technology transfer and workforce development by exposing students to industry perspectives on how computer vision research moves from academic settings into commercial and public-sector applications. Mentors shared insights into applied research, product development, and interdisciplinary collaboration, helping students understand pathways for translating research into real-world impact.

Overall, the award strengthened the computer vision research community by investing in the next generation of researchers and educators. Rather than producing a single technical artifact, the project enhanced the quality, inclusivity, and sustainability of the research ecosystem itself. By supporting student participation, mentorship, and professional growth at WACV 2025, this NSF-funded project advanced both the intellectual foundations of computer vision and its broader societal impact.
